summary : information on non - enron activity
enron policy on outside non - enron activities was revised and re - issued in november of 1999 . the policy prohibits enron employees from engaging in activities that are in conflict with enron ' s business interests without first obtaining approval from the company .
the policy applies to all employees of enron and all employees of enron ' s subsidiaries , including all enron employees who are employees of enron subsidiaries , regardless of the title or capacity in which an employee serves . in addition , the policy applies to all outside activities , including but not limited to membership on another company ' s board of directors , teaching and consulting . the policy applies whether the outside activity involves compensation to the employee or not .
the policy does not apply to charitable , civic , academic and social activities . prior approval is not required prior to engaging in such activities .
the policy is available on the internet at the following address :
http : / / intranet . enron . com / corp / ethics / polnonenr . html
here is a brief summary of the policy :
if you are an enron officer or a vice president , you should discuss the proposed activity with your managing director or evp . if you are a managing director or evp , you should discuss the proposed activity with the office of the chairman .
if you are not an officer or a vice president , you should discuss the proposed activity with your immediate supervisor . your supervisor should consider the proposed activity and determine whether it is in conflict with the business interests of enron . if the supervisor determines that the activity is in conflict with the business interests of enron , then he or she should notify the employee in writing and discuss with the employee whether the activity can be modified so it is not in conflict with the business interests of enron . if the supervisor determines that the activity is not in conflict with the business interests of enron , then he or she can approve the activity by completing the " request for approval of outside non - enron activities " form .
the policy is intended to be flexible to ensure that the employee and enron can identify and address any potential conflict of interest . please call karen watson at 3 - 3979 if you have any questions regarding the policy . thank you for your cooperation .

hello folks ,
i am frequently asked by employees what is the most tax efficient way to exercise their stock options . here is a summary of the tax implications for non - qualified stock options ( nqos ) .
1 . the spread between the fair market value of the stock on the date of exercise and the exercise price is treated as ordinary income . this amount will be reported on your w - 2 in box 1 . this is referred to as the spread or the bargain element and is subject to the usual payroll taxes .
2 . enron will withhold taxes on the spread at the supplemental rate of 27.65 % ( federal plus fica ) . however , the exact amount of taxes that you owe will depend on your overall tax situation and will be determined when you file your tax return .
3 . the first year after exercise you are eligible to sell the stock , you will be able to take advantage of long - term capital gains tax rates . long - term capital gains are currently taxed at a maximum rate of 20 % , while short - term gains are taxed at your ordinary income tax rate . the holding period begins on the day after you exercise your options .
4 . if the stock is sold at a loss , it can be used to offset other capital gains or up to $ 3,000 of ordinary income .
5 . you may want to consult your personal tax advisor to determine the most beneficial tax strategy for you .
6 . you can check the current value of the stock by calling 1 - 800 - 759 - 6416 or go to finance . enron . com and click on stock quote .
7 . you can buy , sell , or exercise your enron stock options by calling 1 - 800 - 688 - 1237 or go to finance . enron . com and click on stock options .
8 . you can find out more information about stock options by going to finance . enron . com and click on stock options .

if you think the stock market is a mess now , wait until the tens of thousands of newly minted millionaires from the 1990s realize they blew it .
what 's the difference between today 's stock market and the tulip frenzy of 17th century holland ? tulip mania , for all its excesses , didn 't make anyone rich . the dot - com bubble , on the other hand , has anointed tens of thousands of new millionaires . the big difference : the tulip bubble popped and that was it . the dot - com bubble is a dud but there is still time to cash in your chips -- if you act fast .
the ( long - winded ) point here is that the 1990s are over and it 's time to get back to basics . over the next few months forbes will be publishing a series of articles about how to manage your money in the new millennium . here are the highlights : - be a contrarian . the best way to beat the market is to go where the crowd is not . this means selling growth stocks and buying value . over the last ten years , growth stocks soared 13 % a year , value stocks 10 % . these days you can get value stocks at a 40 % discount to growth stocks , the biggest gap in 15 years . this means you can buy the likes of boeing , exxon , shell and merck at the same p / e as youd pay for a startup . if you 're in the mutual fund business , buy wellesley income and dodge & cox stock . if you 're an individual investor , buy the stocks at the end of the value 500 list ( pg . 180 of the dec . 18 issue of forbes ) . they 're cheap . there 's a catch : in a roaring bull market , value stocks tend to underperform . but when the market cools , value stocks outperform . and they 're less volatile . they 're also great for the long haul . over 30 years , value stocks have returned 14.3 % , growth stocks 11.4 % . - forget about market timing . the great sin of the 1990s is that the vast majority of investors thought they were smarter than the market . they were not . the best way to invest is the simplest way : dollar - cost - averaging . that is , put a fixed sum of money into a mutual fund every month . over time , your cost basis will be lower than the market price . if you 're nearing retirement and have a huge chunk of your net worth tied up in stocks , you should take some money off the table . but if you 're younger , you are still better off investing regularly in a good mutual fund . you 'll be able to buy more shares when the market dips . market timers are kidding themselves . the evidence is clear : over a ten - year period , they underperform buy - and - hold investors by 4.5 % a year . - focus on asset allocation . the most important thing you can do is make sure your portfolio is properly allocated . that is , determine how much of your money should be in stocks and how much in bonds and cash . the easiest way to do this is to determine what percentage of your portfolio should be in stocks by subtracting your age from 100 . so if you 're 30 , 70 % of your assets should be in stocks . if you 're 60 , 40 % should be in stocks . if you 're 80 , 20 % should be in stocks . then divide your stock allocation among large - cap , small - cap , international and emerging market stocks . the rest should go into bonds and cash . - keep your costs down . the only thing you can control about your portfolio is the costs . these include commissions , fees and taxes . pay attention to all of them . the average mutual fund charges an annual fee of 1.5 % . that 's too high . the vanguard 500 index fund charges .2 % . in a down market

derivatives meet the " common sense " requirements for hedge accounting either .
in my mind , the term " hedge " implies reducing or mitigating a specific
business risk . the derivatives that we executed last week do not really do
that . instead , they are more in the nature of a bet on the future value of
natural gas . if the bet turns out well , enron will record additional earnings
( under the mark - to - market method ) . if the bet turns out poorly , enron will
have to record a loss . if enron had executed the derivatives as a hedge of a
specific identifiable transaction , it might be able to support the economic
hedge argument . for example , if enron had entered into a fixed price gas
purchase agreement in conjunction with the derivatives , it might be able to
argue that the overall position is " riskless " and that the derivatives are
acting as a hedge

The City Council of Monterey Park is considering a proposal to build a new parking garage in downtown Monterey Park . The proposed garage would have 500 spaces and would be located on the corner of Atlantic and Garvey boulevards . The city has been considering the proposal for several months and has held several public hearings on the issue .

The city 's current parking garage , located on the corner of Garfield and Garvey boulevards , has a capacity of only 300 spaces . The proposed garage would more than double the city 's parking capacity and would help to alleviate the parking problems that have plagued the downtown area for years .

The proposed garage has been met with mixed reactions from the community . Some residents are concerned about the impact the garage would have on traffic and the environment . Others are concerned about the cost of the project and the impact it would have on the city 's budget .

The city council will vote on the proposal at its next meeting , which is scheduled for March 15 . If the proposal is approved , construction on the garage is expected to begin later this year .
